NEWPORT, VT. – The Northeastern Vermont Development Association (NVDA) has completed its acquisition of the Newport Development Block, formerly known as “The Pit,” marking an important step forward in the City of Newport’s efforts to return the long-vacant downtown property to productive use. The $1.1 million acquisition, announced in August, proceeded as anticipated and brings the prominent downtown property under local and regional stewardship. The purchase was made possible in part by a $1 million Rural Industry Development Program grant from the Vermont Department of Economic Development, with NVDA providing additional funds to complete the purchase and cover related costs. The immediate next step is to conduct a Phase II environmental assessment, which will determine whether there are contaminants in the soil and if it requires further remediation. This is an essential step to prepare the site for future development. Concurrently, NVDA and the city will work together to identify a developer for the site and advance plans for the property consistent with the priorities outlined in Newport’s 2024 Master Plan. “This is an important milestone for the City of Newport, and NVDA is proud to be a partner in its revitalization efforts,” said David Snedeker, Executive Director of NVDA. “Acquiring the development block was a team effort, but now the real work begins to create something that adds value and vitality to downtown Newport. Newport Mayor Rick-Ufford Chase views this property as having a meaningful role in the city’s future and expressed excitement about the momentum building around it. “We’re thrilled to see this come together as expected, and we’re grateful for NVDA’s partnership and its willingness to take on this important step for Newport.” The Newport Initiative is a collaborative effort that brings together the City of Newport, Newport Downtown Development, community members, local businesses, and regional partners to advance the revitalization of downtown Newport through strategic investment, thoughtful planning, and broad public engagement. Conversely, if it looks like demand for AI accelerator chips is waning, the market sours on Nvidia, and that's what happened last week. Several AI stocks tanked on the news, including Nvidia, which is down 4% since the news came out. That might not sound like a lot, but for a $5 trillion company, it translates into $200 billion. Should retail investors view this as a buying opportunity? Nvidia isn't the only AI chipmaker around, but its chips are critical providers of power for the high-level inference and reasoning that support AI functions. That means all large models require Nvidia chips and, increasingly, full Nvidia compute systems. It recently launched its latest platform, Vera Rubin, which combines Rubin graphics processing units (GPUs), Vera central processing units (CPUs), large quantities of high bandwidth memory, and other hardware to deliver high processing power. The company's revenue growth has recently accelerated, with the top line more than doubling year over year in its fiscal 2027 second quarter (which ended July 26). Management already provided fiscal 2028 guidance for 70% growth, which would be a serious feat given how large the company already is. That 4% drop doesn't on its own create an incredible buying opportunity. However, it might be a good time to buy the stock if you've been planning to anyway. The more pressing concern is what the market is actually worried about: whether OpenAI's news is actually bad news for Nvidia. There's some risk there that investors should keep in mind. Nvidia stock is well-priced right now, trading at less than 14 times forward one-year earnings. I wouldn't make it the central component of your portfolio, but Nvidia looks like a buy right now. (NASDAQ:NVDA) has entered its "manic phase," Pulitzer Prize-winning historian Liaquat Ahamed warned Friday, comparing it to the railroad frenzy that ended in the Panic of 1873. Speaking on the Prof G Markets podcast, Ahamed said competition, overbuilding and debt could undermine returns on the vast sums pouring into data centers, even if the boom continues another year or two. Railroads transformed the economy, but many of the companies financing their expansion went bankrupt. Ahamed traced the crash to Jay Cooke, a powerful banker who raised billions for the Union during the Civil War. Cooke then backed the Northern Pacific, a new transcontinental railroad. With hundreds of miles of track laid, investors assumed he could finance the rest. But in September 1873, Cooke announced he couldn't secure the necessary funding. His firm collapsed, triggering a financial panic. As Ahamed explained, if even Cooke couldn't raise the money, what chance did smaller railroad companies have? Within three months, railroad construction had ground to a halt, and roughly a quarter of U.S. railroad companies defaulted within a year. Ahamed drew a modern parallel: What if OpenAI suddenly couldn't finance its enormous AI commitments? He later identified Oracle as another company potentially vulnerable to a funding crisis. Microsoft Corp. (NASDAQ:MSFT) CEO Satya Nadella has cited Ahamed's book on 1873, saying Microsoft would be careful not to overbuild. Ahamed said Nadella "got the wrong end of the stick." Individual railroad companies weren't necessarily reckless. Each kept expanding because slowing down meant surrendering business to competitors. "It's the collectivity of their decisions that leads to overbuilding," he said. Ahamed identified three warning signs before the railroad crash: excess capacity, eroding profitability and more expensive financing. He said much of today's AI borrowing remains opaque. He described Nvidia as "essentially lending to its customers," although its arrangements also involve equity investments and purchase commitments rather than conventional loans. Nvidia has invested in CoreWeave Inc. (NASDAQ:CRWV) and entered a $6.3 billion agreement to purchase qualifying unused computing capacity through 2032. Some CoreWeave bonds yielded around 16% this week amid mounting debt concerns. Nvidia shares fell 1.8% Thursday amid the broader AI-stock selloff. On Polymarket, traders put the probability of a defined AI downturn by Dec. 31 at roughly 7%. The contract requires at least three specified stress events. That low probability is consistent with Ahamed's view that the boom could run another year or two. Financial crises, he noted, tend to "take much longer to happen than you imagined" before they "happen much faster than you thought they could." title: Germany Reportedly Picks Nvidia for Its Industrial AI Push, but the Money Barely Matters - TIKR.com
content: Mariia Demchenko from Getty Images Nana Dua from Pexels via Canva Nvidia (NVDA) is reportedly lining up another government partnership in Europe. Germany plans a wide-ranging cooperation agreement with Nvidia to push AI deeper into German industry, Reuters reported on Thursday, October 15, citing the business daily Handelsblatt. The deal is expected to be unveiled next week at the government’s Invest in Germany Summit in Berlin, which CEO Jensen Huang will attend. Government sources confirmed the plan to Reuters on Friday, October 16, saying Germany will announce the agreement next week with partners beyond Nvidia. The funding, the participants and the terms still rest on Handelsblatt’s reporting, and nothing official has been published. Handelsblatt says the agreement has two goals. The first is to lay the groundwork for physical AI, meaning the tools used to train robots and self-driving vehicles. The second is to build high-performance AI models for industry. That work would run through SOOFI (Sovereign Open Source Foundation Models), a German project launched last year with universities, research institutes and AI companies. Berlin would put in hundreds of millions of euros for computing power and model training, and Nvidia would send engineers. About 12 German companies are expected to join. They include Siemens (SIEGY), Audi (owned by Volkswagen (VWAGY)) and the AI startup Black Forest Labs. Start with the size of the deal. Nvidia booked $302.97 billion in revenue over the last 12 months, after its revenue roughly doubled this year. Suppose Germany spent a full €1 billion and every euro went to Nvidia hardware. That would still be under 0.4% of the total. The business this deal targets is bigger than Nvidia’s segment table suggests. In fiscal 2026, which ended in January, the Automotive segment made $2.35 billion, or 1.1% of total revenue, against $193.74 billion from Data Center. But CFO Colette Kress said on the February earnings call that physical AI brought in more than $6 billion that year, and Nvidia put the figure above $9 billion over the trailing 12 months when it reported in May. That puts physical AI at more than roughly 3.5% of Nvidia’s sales over the same 12 months. Automotive, the one piece of it Nvidia broke out, grew 39% last fiscal year, against 68% for Data Center. For Nvidia, the money matters less than whose tools German industry trains on. Siemens is already building a joint industrial AI operating system with Nvidia, announced at CES in January. Deutsche Telekom (DTEGY) runs an industrial AI cloud with Nvidia under a €1 billion partnership, with Nvidia supplying 10,000 GPUs. That cloud already hosts SOOFI: Leibniz Universität Hannover hired Telekom to supply the project’s computing infrastructure. That makes it a likely home for any new compute spending, though no allocation has been reported. Manufacturers that train robots on Nvidia’s software today are the likeliest buyers of its chips for those robots later. Some of that shows up in Edge Computing, which made $7.2 billion in the July quarter, up 27%. That category also holds PCs, game consoles and workstations, though, so it doesn’t isolate robots and cars. The reports don’t say how much of the money becomes Nvidia revenue, and the split may not settle it. Telekom’s cloud has run on Nvidia hardware since February, so renting more of its capacity pays Telekom first. Nvidia gains only if the extra demand forces new chip purchases or software deals. Research grants to SOOFI can end up buying computing time too. Either way, the deal won’t move Nvidia’s numbers. The detail to listen for in Berlin next week is whether Siemens, Audi and the other companies commit their own spending on top of the state’s money. If they do, a government program turns into a customer pipeline for Nvidia’s physical AI business. Want to see how small Nvidia’s car and robot business is next to its data center sales? title: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella Just Shared Bad News for Nvidia and Great News for This Rival Chipmaker - The Motley Fool
content: New plans for Azure could leave less room for Nvidia. Microsoft (MSFT -1.93%) is planning a big change to its Azure cloud computing data centers starting next year. It will rely much more on its custom-designed silicon than on leading graphics processing units (GPUs) like those from Nvidia (NVDA -1.43%). It's already made significant progress in expanding workloads for its Maia 200 chips, and it expects its next-generation Maia 300 chips to deliver significant improvements when it starts deploying them next year. "Starting next calendar year, we will scale our Maia family to multi-gigawatt deployments, making it the primary inference system for our own product and services," CEO Satya Nadella said.  That's great news for its custom chip partner, Marvell Technology (MRVL -5.56%), and bad news for Nvidia. Nvidia's extreme dominance of the data center GPU space during the first few years of the artificial intelligence (AI) boom left its market share with nowhere to go but down. Its biggest customers, including the hyperscalers and leading AI frontier labs, have developed custom solutions that can handle AI workloads, and that can deliver better price performance on specific tasks than Nvidia's GPUs. That said, GPUs offer far greater flexibility in terms of the types of tasks they can perform, making them particularly valuable for companies deploying servers to sell compute capacity to third parties with dynamic demands. Notice that Microsoft is starting its Maia expansion by focusing on its own products and services, not on leasing Maia compute capacity to third parties looking to cut costs on their OpenAI GPT-based applications. Their use, though, could expand over the long run. Alphabet (GOOG -2.32%) (GOOGL -2.47%), which has been building its own custom AI chips for longer than any of its competitors, has seen strong adoption of its Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) by its Google Cloud customers for training and inference. title: Mercedes-Benz and NVIDIA Expand Strategic Partnership to Advance Safe Highly Automated Driving in the Next Decade - NVIDIA Newsroom
content:
Mercedes-Benz and NVIDIA today announced that they will extend their strategic partnership to advance the next generation of automated driving systems. The collaboration brings together Mercedes-Benz’s automotive engineering and safety expertise and its MB.OS operating system with NVIDIA’s accelerated computing and AI technologies. “NVIDIA is our most important strategic partner in automated driving. Together, we developed the first Mercedes-Benz assistance system for urban point-to-point driving for the western world,” Jörg Burzer, member of the board of management of Mercedes‑Benz Group AG and chief technology officer, development and procurement. “The expansion of our partnership marks a significant milestone and reflects the mutual trust we have built over the years. Together, we aim to bring further pioneering innovations to the road, offering our customers the best automated driving experience while upholding the high safety standards they expect from a Mercedes-Benz.” “Accelerated computing is giving vehicles the intelligence to understand the world and reason through complex driving situations,” said Ali Kani, vice president of automotive at NVIDIA. “Mercedes-Benz brings the engineering excellence and commitment to safety this transformation demands. Together, we’re building on NVIDIA Hyperion to bring that intelligence and full-stack safety to the road and make autonomous driving an everyday reality.” Mercedes-Benz’s MB.OS operating system supports new driving functions and over-the-air updates, working with NVIDIA Hyperion’s in-vehicle computing and sensor architecture. NVIDIA Alpamayo Stack provides full-stack driving software with AI reasoning capabilities, supporting point-to-point urban assistance, active safety and automated parking. NVIDIA Halos adds to the Mercedes-Benz safety foundation, including a parallel safety stack that adds redundancy and guardrails. Together, these technologies support advanced driver assistance and the development of future SAE-Level 4 applications, including robolimousines. Beyond automated driving, Mercedes-Benz also relies on NVIDIA technologies for vehicle engineering simulation and within MO360, its digital production ecosystem — from virtual planning to AI-based applications. The two partners are working to further enhance efficiency, flexibility and quality across the global production network. About NVIDIA

Lenders are getting nervous about CoreWeave (NASDAQ:CRWV), a cloud company that rents out artificial intelligence (AI) chips made by Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA). In June, CoreWeave sold $1.25 billion in unsecured notes due 2032 at face value, with a 9.625% coupon. On Tuesday, Oct. 13, the yield on these notes reportedly reached almost 15% before ending at a record of around 14.5%. A bond's yield climbs when the price drops. Put another way, bond buyers now want much more to lend to CoreWeave than they did four months ago. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » The stock followed on Wednesday. CoreWeave shares dropped about 15% as of this writing, and Nvidia, which is both CoreWeave's chip supplier and one of its shareholders, fell about 3% to roughly $221. Should Nvidia investors worry? I don't think so -- at least not about CoreWeave itself. What Nvidia directly has riding on CoreWeave turns out to be small next to what the chipmaker earns. CoreWeave's trouble doesn't seem to be demand. Showing how quickly the business is still growing, CoreWeave's second-quarter revenue more than doubled year over year to around $2.6 billion. But the company lost $49 million on an operating basis, and its net interest expense of $640 million was more than twice what it was in the year-ago quarter. Its total debt was around $35.6 billion at midyear. Simply put, CoreWeave is still borrowing to buy its chips, and it doesn't yet make enough from operations to pay its interest costs. The most direct link is Nvidia's stake. Nvidia owned about 47.2 million CoreWeave shares on June 30, according to its latest holdings report. That position was worth about $4.7 billion then. At Wednesday's price of around $66, it's worth more like $3.1 billion. And the roughly 23 million shares Nvidia bought in January, for $87.20 each, are off about 24%. Nvidia also has a capacity deal with CoreWeave. In September 2025, the two companies signed an order with an initial value of $6.3 billion. Under it, Nvidia must buy any CoreWeave cloud capacity that CoreWeave's own customers don't use, through April 2032, subject to some conditions. Of course, this backstop might cost Nvidia the most if CoreWeave's customers leave, which arguably isn't happening while revenue is doubling. Nvidia's latest quarterly filing doesn't name CoreWeave at all. But it does show $36 billion in commitments under deals with AI cloud partners, usually six years long, and up to $3.5 billion in guarantees on some of those partners' data center leases. It also lists a maximum possible loss of $4.7 billion from certain stakes in infrastructure financiers (companies that help fund AI infrastructure). Together, those items come to about $44 billion spread across several years -- and the filing doesn't say how much involves CoreWeave. (The filing's far bigger guarantee, up to $105 billion on data center leases linked to an OpenAI affiliate, is another matter.) For context, Nvidia made $63.7 billion in operating income in its second quarter of fiscal 2027 alone (the three months ended July 26, 2026). CoreWeave's purchases might be a small part of Nvidia's sales, too. CoreWeave spent around $14.1 billion on property and equipment in the first half of 2026, and not all of it went to Nvidia. In roughly the same period, Nvidia's revenue was around $178 billion. Even if every dollar of CoreWeave's spending had gone to Nvidia, it'd be under 8% of Nvidia's sales. Meanwhile, Nvidia's profits are still climbing quickly. Its operating income grew 124% year over year in fiscal Q2, and it was up around 19% from $53.5 billion in fiscal Q1. Yes, the bigger risk isn't CoreWeave alone. If lenders pull back from every debt-funded AI cloud company at once, orders for Nvidia's chips might slow. Yet the stock arguably already assumes some slowdown. Nvidia's price-to-earnings ratio is only around 14, using analysts' average earnings estimate for fiscal 2028 (Nvidia's next fiscal year). I think that's a low price for a company whose operating income just more than doubled. In the end, CoreWeave's bond prices are a fair warning of how much of the AI build-out runs on debt. But Nvidia's own exposure to CoreWeave is small next to what the chipmaker earns in one quarter. I'd still buy Nvidia stock at this price, albeit in a size appropriate to the high-risk nature of a growth stock like this. Nvidia (NVDA) CEO Jensen Huang is unlikely to ignore the building pressure on CoreWeave's (CRWV) stock price and bond values. The simple reason is that he can't look the other way, given how intertwined Nvidia is with the most well-known — and debated — neocloud. First, in January of this year, Nvidia announced an expansion of its relationship with CoreWeave. The deal included Nvidia investing $2 billion in CoreWeave stock. CoreWeave committed to using Nvidia's technology to build more than 5 gigawatts of AI factories by 2030. Nvidia now holds 47.2 million shares of CoreWeave stock, or around 10% of the company. Second, CoreWeave is a huge customer of Nvidia, as shown in the chart below from the team at Boring Business. CoreWeave buys GPUs from Nvidia and then rents that compute out to other companies, including hyperscalers like Meta (META). "0% chance $NVDA lets $CRWV falter," tech analyst Daniel Newman said on X. Yet, CoreWeave's failure is what the market is chatting about. CoreWeave stock plunged 6% in premarket trading on Thursday following a 15% rout on Wednesday. "In our view, the company's long-term business model remains economically challenged; we maintain our Underperform," Bernstein analyst Madison Rezaei said in a note Thursday. Read more: Why CoreWeave stock may still rise over 100% despite financing fears, analyst says Two factors collided to spark Wednesday's sell-off. One, CoreWeave's corporate bonds across maturities continued to be dumped amid fears of an AI slowdown and its implications for the company's precarious balance sheet. The rise in yields on CoreWeave's bonds even spurred Elon Musk to post "Yikes" on X in response to a post by venture capitalist Chamath Palihapitiya. The selling spread to other AI cloud stocks: Nebius (NBIS) fell 11%, Oracle (ORCL) dropped another 9%, and the following stocks sank more than 10%: DigitalOcean (DOCN), Hut 8 (HUT), Cipher (CIFR), TeraWulf (WULF), and IREN (IREN). Read more: Why CoreWeave stock may still rise over 100% despite financing fears, analyst says Two, Gartner, in a new report, forecast that by 2030 "cost pressure and a lack of a differentiating business model will force over 80% of neocloud providers to cease independent operations." CoreWeave is a neocloud. The report essentially was akin to yelling "fire" in a crowded theater. At some point soon, Nvidia's Huang may have to step in and comment on Nvidia's confidence in CoreWeave. He has a financial interest in doing so, not only from an Nvidia standpoint, but also from the viewpoint of the wider AI boom his company's chips are fueling. title: History Says Nvidia Stock Usually Rises in the Fourth Quarter -- It Has in 20 of the Last 27 - The Motley Fool
content: Two of the seven down years erased over half the stock's value. What went wrong? Shares of Nvidia (NVDA -1.43%) hit another record on Tuesday, Oct. 6, closing at $239.24. If history's any guide, the October-to-December quarter has usually been a good one for the artificial intelligence (AI) chip giant's stock. Measured from the end of September to the end of December, Nvidia's shares rose in 20 of the 27 years from 1999 through 2025. The median change for all 27 fourth quarters was a gain of around 14%. But the record comes with two caveats. Nvidia's stock has climbed in most quarters during this stretch, not just the last one of the year. From 2000 through 2025, for example, it also gained in 20 of 26 first quarters. And two of the seven fourth quarters that went wrong cost shareholders over half their money. I think the calendar matters much less here than the report Nvidia puts out in the middle of it. Nvidia's fiscal year ends in late January, so its fiscal third quarter closes in late October. The report for that period tends to come in mid-to-late November, about halfway through the calendar fourth quarter. That report also gives management's revenue outlook for the fiscal fourth quarter, which runs roughly from November through January. Sure, even a great report doesn't promise a good quarter. Nvidia's fiscal third-quarter 2026 results, released Nov. 19, 2025, showed revenue up 62% year over year to $57.0 billion. Management also guided for $65.0 billion in the next quarter. The stock dropped around 3% a day later. It closed the fourth quarter down 0.04% -- a paper-thin loss in a quarter when the Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC -2.15%) gained around 3%. Nvidia's two worst fourth quarters broke the pattern for very different reasons. In 2000, the stock lost 60% as the dot-com crash pulled down tech stocks broadly. The Nasdaq Composite slid by around a third during the same three months. But Nvidia's shares were back above their late-September 2000 price by April 2001. The 2018 decline was mainly Nvidia's own problem, and the November report made it far worse. By report day, shares had already fallen about 28% from their late-September close. For the three months ended Oct. 28, 2018 (Nvidia's fiscal third quarter of 2019), revenue grew 21% year over year to $3.18 billion. But management forecast fiscal fourth-quarter revenue of $2.70 billion, around 15% below what the company had just reported. "Our near-term results reflect excess channel inventory post the cryptocurrency boom, which will be corrected," CEO Jensen Huang said in the earnings release. Put simply, too many of Nvidia's chips sat unsold with distributors and retailers after demand from cryptocurrency miners cooled. Shares fell about 19% the day after the report and ended the quarter down 52%, versus a loss of about 18% for the Nasdaq. They didn't climb back above their late-September 2018 close till February 2020. Notably, most of Nvidia's down fourth quarters lined up with a falling market. The Nasdaq fell in five of the seven. Only in 2020 and last year did Nvidia's shares drop while the index gained. Nvidia's business now looks nothing like it did in late 2018. For its fiscal second quarter of 2027 (which ended on July 26, 2026), revenue more than doubled, climbing 106% year over year to $96.2 billion. Management's forecast calls for $108.0 billion in fiscal Q3, plus or minus 2%. That's the bar the fiscal third-quarter report needs to clear. Meeting the guide would mean growth of about 89% from the $57.0 billion Nvidia reported a year earlier, a step down from 106%. The forecast for the following quarter could matter even more to the stock than the quarter itself. Nvidia's shares sell for around 15 times the consensus earnings estimate for fiscal 2028 (the year ending January 2028). Broadcom, another AI chipmaker, costs about 19 times its consensus earnings estimate for its next fiscal year. True, a price-to-earnings ratio is only as good as the estimates behind it. But at that price, Nvidia's shares could arguably weather a weaker report than the past few. So, does the calendar make Nvidia stock a buy right now? Not on its own. Twenty up years out of 27 mainly reflect a stock that's climbed in most quarters, whatever the season. And the worst years that broke the pattern saw a falling market, a weak forecast from Nvidia, or both. At today's price, I'd consider buying shares for the growth Nvidia is delivering. The fourth quarter's history doesn't do much for that case. Daniel Sparks and his clients do not have positions in any of the stocks mentioned.
